title: Moules marinières
subtitle: Mussels steamed in white wine and shallots
excerpt: Fresh mussels steamed open in white wine, shallots, and parsley until the broth is fragrant and saline. The French classic that asks almost nothing of the cook except good mussels and a large enough pot.
sourceNotes: Classic French bistro preparation. Auguste Escoffier, Le Guide Culinaire (1903) describes moules marinières as a standard preparation for live mussels with white wine and aromatics. The dish appears throughout Normandy and Brittany coastal cookery.

content.text: Moules marinières is mussels steamed open in a wide pot with white wine, shallots, and parsley. The mussels cook in under 5 minutes once the liquid is hot, and the broth they release as they open is saline and deeply flavoured. You eat it with the shells as spoons and a good amount of bread.

attrs.title: Buying and preparing mussels
attrs.body: Buy mussels on the day you plan to eat them. They should smell of the sea, not of ammonia. Discard any that are open and do not close when tapped sharply on the work surface. After cooking, discard any that have not opened. Scrub the shells under cold water, debeard by pulling away the threads from the hinge, and they are ready.

items.prepNote: scrubbed and debearded, discard any that won't close

content.text: Melt half the butter in a large, deep pot over medium heat. Add the shallots and cook for 3 minutes until softened. Add the garlic and cook for 1 more minute.
Pour in the wine and bring to a fast simmer.
Add all the mussels at once. Clamp on the lid. Cook over high heat for 4 to 5 minutes, shaking the pot once or twice. The mussels are done when the shells have opened.
Lift the mussels into wide bowls, leaving the broth in the pot. Discard any mussels that have not opened.
Swirl the remaining butter into the hot broth. Add the parsley and a good grind of pepper. Pour the broth over the mussels and serve at once with plenty of bread.

items.symptom: Many mussels have not opened after cooking
items.cause: The mussels were dead before cooking, or the pot was not hot enough
items.fix: Discard any that won't open; do not try to prise them. Ensure the pot is at a hard boil before the lid goes on.

items.symptom: The broth is gritty with sand
items.cause: The mussels were not scrubbed thoroughly
items.fix: Serve the broth from the top of the pot, leaving the sandy sediment behind. Scrub shells more vigorously next time.

items.symptom: The mussels taste tough and rubbery
items.fix: Mussels need only 4 to 5 minutes. Remove the lid the moment the shells open and serve straight away.
Add the remaining butter to round it out. Use a wine you would drink; the broth will reflect its quality.

content.text: Moules marinières is the signature seafood dish of the French coast from Normandy to the Basque Country. It is served in every bistro and brasserie as a main course for one, typically in a large copper pot with frites. At home it makes a quick and impressive dinner: most of the work is in the preparation of the mussels, and the cook time is barely 10 minutes from first mussel to table.
